div.head: Chapter 20
div.p: The second reason or conjecture is: because in order for unjust wars and the robberies, injuries, deaths, and captivities that are always inflicted on one's neighbors in them to be excusable, and for those who wage them not to be guilty of them and placed in bad faith until it is established — when they are in doubt — whether they are justly or unjustly moved and carried out, and when their injustice or iniquity is not clearly established, it is required that they be done by the command and authority of their king or prince, of whom they are properly vassals and subjects, and that the king summon them and command them to go and serve him in such a war or carry out such a measure of justice; those who are thus summoned and commanded by their prince, so long as the truth of the justice is not known, even if the wars are unjust and the robberies and killings commanded to be done are carried out unjustly, are excused from sin, and also from the obligation to restore what was acquired by that cause, because obedience to their proper prince or king excuses them in such doubt, as Saint Augustine and the saints say: c. 23, q. 1, c. quid culpatur. And even in this case, when they are summoned and commanded by their prince, the said subjects must, if a doubt about the war arises for them, inquire and ask the most wise and God-fearing persons — those without suspicion of interest, such as were described — for the truth; and if such persons were to certify them of the injustice of that war, they would then be obliged not to obey the command of the prince, even if they had to lose their lives on that account. And concerning this point, without asking persons such as those described, subjects might see and have such and so manifest signs and indications of the injustice and iniquity of such wars or of the prince's command, that obedience to the prince would not excuse them: just as if the prince commanded that all clergy be stripped of their goods, or that monasteries be sacked, or likewise that peaceful towns be robbed, and if it were known to everyone that they did not know such an act was unjust, they would not be excused. For such ignorance is called crass and willful, which is no excuse; or affected, which aggravates the sins. For otherwise, the Jews who killed the Son of God as man would have been excused, and the gentiles in persecuting and killing the martyrs. But the contrary reason applies to those who are not summoned and commanded by their prince, but of their own will and for their own greed and interests involve themselves and volunteer for such wars and deeds, from which deaths and harms to their neighbors necessarily arise, and which happen to be unjust: because obedience does not excuse such persons in cases of doubt, as has been proved; and therefore, before putting themselves in that danger, they are obliged to inform themselves of the truth of the doubt and resolve it, being certified that that deed and exercise are lawful and just. And if they are negligent in this and take no care of it out of stupid and brutish simplicity, they are always in bad faith and live beyond all doubt in mortal sin. So that, without being in a state of eternal damnation, they cannot volunteer for or carry out such deeds and exercises.

And this applies all the more in wars, where the harms and irreparable evils that neighbors receive are so certain, necessary, and most grave, such as deaths, captivities, and despoiling of temporal goods; and if they are kingdoms of foreign lords, usurpation of dominions. The reason why it is mortal sin to act in such doubt is that they deviate from right reason, and insofar as it is in themselves, they love that thing more than God and despise the divine precept, choosing rather to carry out that dangerous deed with the doubt of incurring the violation of the divine law, than to abstain from the said deed with certainty of not erring or offending God. And this is the general rule of all the Doctors: that both subjects and non-subjects, both those summoned and commanded and those not summoned or commanded, who are so disposed as to go to wars or to other exercises dangerous to their neighbors, not caring about the justice or injustice of such war or deed, but with their eye fixed on acquiring money however they can get it, there is no doubt whatsoever that such persons are always in mortal sin.

Applying, then, everything said to our present purpose in this truth, let all confessors be certain, because by it they will be able to answer many frivolous arguments and confound and dismantle many false and feigned excuses that some put forward in such execrable and most cruel devastations and acts of theft: that the kings of Castile never provoked or commanded that any person should go to the Indies to make war upon those peoples whom they knew to be by their nature peaceable, whether with wages or without, whether out of fear or promises, or by their command or authority; it was never done, except at the very beginning when those lands were discovered, when the Catholic King and Queen sent a certain number of people at wages — not to make war or rob or take from the Indians what was theirs, nor to kill them or enslave them —, but solely to settle on the island of Hispaniola, and so that a quicker way could be found for the conversion of those souls. Rather, all those who have gone to those kingdoms have themselves volunteered and offered themselves rashly and blindly, pressing upon the kings and their council to give them license to cross there, with the aim not of saving souls but of acquiring riches; and whether with the intent of obtaining them justly or unjustly, their deeds in the destruction and ruin of those so great kingdoms give truthful testimony.

Great numbers of people crossed to the Indies through the invention that Satan devised, in this manner: a tyrant would come with ten or twelve thousand castellanos or ducats, or more, that he had robbed by many means through the killing of Indians, and would offer himself to the king or his council, saying that for his royal service he wished to go to discover and settle such a province at his own cost, and that they should make him an adelantado and grant him the other favors he asked for, which were assigned to be paid out of the hides of the Indians he was going to rob and kill — on account of the very great and not little culpable ignorance that then prevailed throughout all Spain. This person, arriving in Seville, would preach of great riches and extensive treasures to be found in the land, where everyone was going to prosper. With this hope the people who wanted to would come, and having arrived in the land their business was never anything other than beginning their entry — first, as hungry wolves among most gentle sheep or lambs —: to plunder, tear apart, kill, rob, and thrust free peoples into the servitude of the repartimiento, besides making slaves for buying and selling, as was said in the seventh principle. So that these people were not unaware that the king was not commanding them to cross to the Indies, but that this tyrant was preaching to them and persuading them to cross, promising them great loads of gold and riches.

Likewise, they were not ignorant of this, nor could they be in doubt about it — since doubt, as was said, is to be suspended and indifferent between both contrary positions —: it is plain that they inclined or ought to have inclined to believe that they were not being sent by the king to wage such cruel wars, nor to rob the Indians who were in their homes and doing harm to no one; because such a war was never proclaimed in Seville or anywhere else, nor had such a license to rob and kill them been granted when they were recruited and persuaded; for the tyrant captain would not have dared to proclaim it publicly, since he himself carried the royal provisions forbidding it; albeit, as is believed and even known, he concealed and dissembled the king's provisions and instructions, and privately told them or gave them hope of ruling and robbing with expanded powers; and this was sufficient to place them in bad faith and perverse conscience.

And according to the Doctors on cap. sicut, the 3rd, De jurejurando, "when a war is moved by the authority of someone who is not a prince, it must always be presumed to be unjust when there is doubt; and according to Hostiensis in that chapter, even when it is by the authority of a prince, when the matter is in doubt, it must always be presumed to be unjust." And this appears to be all the more true when the matter is to be treated in the forum of conscience. For the safe course must be followed in such a case according to all the Doctors, above all the theologians. The reason is that since in wars there is nothing done but killing, robbing, enslaving, and inflicting irreparable harms on neighbors, if there is no cause — not one that is pretextual or feigned but one that truly excuses them — one always sins mortally and is under obligation to make restitution, being expressly against the fifth and seventh precepts of the Decalogue. But if the wars they waged against those peoples had been publicly proclaimed, they might have presumed and believed that the king was ordering them to be made. Though even this would not hold, because everyone knew — whether little or much, there or here — that the king prohibited by his provisions and instructions the wars, commanding that so many and such summons first be given which none of them observed; and from the character of the captain's person, and from the words they heard from him, and from the deeds they saw him do, and afterwards from the gentleness of those peoples and the cruelties they inflicted upon them, and from many other circumstances, and from their own intentions and deeds and their own consciences, and from the law of the understanding which is synderesis — the habit that contains the precepts of natural law, which are to do no injustice or injury or wrong to anyone, but rather to do good to all and give to each what is theirs, and not to usurp what belongs to them, nor to offend God, etc. —, and since it is impossible that any man in the world should be ignorant of these precepts by the light that each one has impressed in his soul, they could and should have understood how unjust and diabolical was the exercise and office they were engaged in and the satanic works they were committing.

Since, then, all the Spaniards who have crossed to the Indies went to them without being moved or summoned or commanded or compelled by the kings of Castile, but of their own free will and greed offered and volunteered themselves and importuned the crown for licenses to cross there, as has been said, and found themselves in person and did find themselves in the wars and killings and captivities and other wrongs and irreparable harms they inflicted on those peaceful peoples: it follows that, even if they were in doubt as to whether such wars and the said abominable deeds committed in them were just or moved by just cause, they were obliged, under pain of incurring most grave mortal sins, before going to the Indies, or at least before finding themselves in them and perpetrating such deeds, to inquire and ask the truth of learned and unimpeachable persons, as was said, and not to go; or, since they were already there, not to assist in them nor to be participants in so much bloodshed with any doubt whatsoever, but only with certainty that they contained no injustice. For obedience did not excuse them from the outset; and because they did not do so, and it is certain that everything done in the Indies has been tyrannical and iniquitous, as the whole world — unless they are brutish men — testifies; therefore all of them were guilty of all the wars, all the killings, the devastations, robberies, captivities, despoilings, injustices, wrongs, and mortal sins committed in the said wars; and they did not have good faith but bad faith and perverse conscience, and if they plead ignorance they do not speak the truth, and if they had any ignorance it was affected, or at the very least crass and willful.
